source.title: [BUG] [Info] Unauthenticated /api/rpc/<chain> proxy returns upstream provider errors verbatim, disclosing the backend vendor, subscription plan and internal implementation details
source.body:
## Executive Summary

**Vulnerability Title**: The test-app's unauthenticated JSON-RPC proxy (/api/rpc/<chain>) passes upstream provider error objects through to any client unchanged, disclosing the backend vendor (Alchemy), its subscription tier and limits, and internal library/type details of the node stack

**Severity**: Info

**CVSS Score**: 5.3 - CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N (indicative mapping for an information disclosure)

**Affected Component**: Web App / API (https://test-app.dex223.io/api/rpc/<chain>)

**Discovery Date**: 2026-11-20

**Researcher**: bothuntxyz

**Scope Verification**: This is not the already-reported Alchemy exposure. Issue #71 is a production Alchemy API key sitting in a public JavaScript bundle; no key is disclosed here, and the fix for #71 (removing the key from the bundle) does not touch this behaviour. It is also not #113 (proxy rate limits keyed by a spoofable X-Forwarded-For entry) and not #103 (Next.js image optimizer SSRF and proxy rate-limiter spoofing): the mechanism here is error-object passthrough on the RPC proxy itself. The endpoint is part of the in-scope test-app backend.

## Vulnerability Details

### Description

The swap interface talks to the chain through the app's own JSON-RPC proxy at /api/rpc/<chain> (for example /api/rpc/mainnet). The proxy forwards requests to the upstream provider and returns error responses exactly as the provider produced them, with no mapping or scrubbing. Three classes of detail leak to any unauthenticated client:

1. Provider identity, plan and quota. A wide-range eth_getLogs call returns the provider's own plan text: "Under the Free tier plan, you can make eth_getLogs requests with up to a 10 block range. ... Upgrade to PAYG for expanded block range." An attacker learns the vendor, that the deployment runs on the free tier, and the exact log-range limit, which is directly useful for planning quota abuse against the app's backend.
2. Internal implementation details. Malformed parameters return the node stack's typed errors, including Rust/alloy internals such as "data did not match any variant of untagged enum Variadic", "number too large to fit in target type" and "invalid digit found in string". This fingerprints the backend implementation precisely.
3. Node-level mempool errors. eth_sendRawTransaction errors are echoed unmodified ("insufficient funds for gas * price + value: have 0 want 21000000000000"), confirming live forwarding to the real mainnet mempool and exposing node-side evaluation detail.

The frontend only needs success results and a generic failure signal. Nothing in the UI depends on the provider's error text, so the passthrough is pure disclosure with no functional need.

### Impact Assessment
- **Technical Impact**: Any unauthenticated client can fingerprint the backend provider, its paid-plan status and limits, and the node implementation family, using ordinary malformed RPC calls.
- **Data Impact**: No keys, credentials or user data are exposed. The disclosure is operational metadata about the backend.
- **Business Impact**: The free-tier limits revealed in the errors tell an attacker exactly how cheap it is to exhaust the app's RPC quota, which would degrade the swap interface for all users.
- **User Impact**: None directly. Indirectly, quota exhaustion planned with the leaked limits would surface as failing quotes and balances in the UI.
- **Financial Impact**: None directly.

### Attack Vector

1. Send a JSON-RPC request to https://test-app.dex223.io/api/rpc/mainnet with an eth_getLogs range wider than 10 blocks. Read the provider, plan and limit from the error message.
2. Send requests with deliberately malformed parameters (bad address format, oversized hex values). Collect the internal type errors to fingerprint the node stack.
3. Optionally submit a signed but unfunded raw transaction and read the node-level mempool error, confirming live mainnet forwarding.

No account, wallet or authentication is needed at any step.

### Prerequisites
- Network access to the public test-app. Nothing else.

## Proof of Concept

### Code/Commands

Case 1, provider plan and limits:

```bash
curl -s -X POST https://test-app.dex223.io/api/rpc/mainnet -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"eth_getLogs","params":[{"fromBlock":"0x193a731","toBlock":"0x193ab19","topics":["0x1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef"]}],"id":1}'
```

Response (HTTP 400):

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32600,"message":"Under the Free tier plan, you can make eth_getLogs requests with up to a 10 block range. Based on your parameters, this block range should work: [0x193a731, 0x193a73a]. Upgrade to PAYG for expanded block range."}}
```

Case 2, internal type details. An eth_getLogs call with an invalid address value ("0xzz") returns HTTP 200 with:

```json
{"error":{"code":-32602,"message":"Invalid params","data":"Invalid variadic value or array type: data did not match any variant of untagged enum Variadic at line 1 column 66"}}
```

An oversized hex block number returns "number too large to fit in target type" in the same field.

Case 3, node mempool error. Submitting a validly signed transaction from an empty account via eth_sendRawTransaction returns HTTP 200 with:

```json
{"error":{"code":-32003,"message":"insufficient funds for gas * price + value: have 0 want 21000000000000"}}
```

### Verified output

All three cases were captured as bound request/response traffic during the original scan (4 traffic snapshots on the finding). An independent retest session then re-ran the reproduction against the live app and returned the verdict "reproduced", so the behaviour is confirmed twice, on 2026-11-20.

### Test Environment
- **URL**: https://test-app.dex223.io/api/rpc/mainnet
- **Smart Contract Address**: n/a
- **Test Account**: none (unauthenticated)

## Technical Analysis

### Root Cause

The proxy treats upstream responses as opaque pass-through payloads, including the error branch. JSON-RPC already defines standard error codes and generic messages for these situations; the provider's verbose error text is meant for the API key holder, not for anonymous front-end clients. Because the proxy adds no error-mapping layer, every upstream diagnostic becomes public.

### Affected Code

Server-side proxy handler for /api/rpc/<chain> in the test-app backend (the deployed Next.js app; the handler forwards the upstream response body unchanged on both success and error paths).

### Exploitability
- **Difficulty**: Easy. Plain curl requests.
- **Reliability**: Always. The passthrough is deterministic for any error-producing request.
- **Automation**: Fully automated. Error classes can be enumerated with a small request matrix.

## Remediation

### Suggested Fix

Map errors at the proxy. On an upstream error, return a generic JSON-RPC error with the standard code for the class (for example -32602 for invalid params, -32000 for execution failures) and a fixed message such as "RPC request failed", and log the provider's original error server-side only. Keep the success path unchanged.

### Code Example

```ts
// inside the /api/rpc/<chain> handler, after the upstream call
if (upstreamBody?.error) {
  console.error('upstream rpc error', upstreamBody.error); // server-side only
  return Response.json({
    jsonrpc: '2.0',
    id,
    error: { code: upstreamBody.error.code ?? -32000, message: 'RPC request failed' },
  });
}
```

### Alternative Solutions

An allowlist of safe error messages for the few cases the UI genuinely distinguishes (for example a revert with a user-facing reason on eth_call) would keep useful signal while dropping provider and implementation detail. Rate limiting the proxy per client would additionally blunt the quota-abuse planning this disclosure enables, and complements the existing rate-limit work rather than replacing this fix.

## Additional Information

### Related Vulnerabilities

#71 (Alchemy API key in the JS bundle), #113 (proxy rate limits keyed by spoofable X-Forwarded-For) and #103 (image optimizer SSRF, proxy rate-limiter spoofing) touch the same surface but are different mechanisms; see Scope Verification.

### References
- CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
- CWE-201: Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data
- OWASP: Improper Error Handling

### Timeline
- **Discovery**: 2026-11-20
- **Verification**: 2026-11-20 (original capture plus an independent retest, verdict reproduced)
- **Report Submission**: pending (filed by the researcher)

## Researcher Information

**Name**: bothuntxyz

**Preferred Payment Method**: D223 Tokens only

**Disclosure Preference**: Public, per the program's tracker rules

## Environment

Live target https://test-app.dex223.io (in-scope web property of the Dex223 Bug Bounty Program), tested 2026-11-20 with plain HTTPS requests; no account or wallet was used. The finding was produced by an authorised scan of the in-scope app and re-verified by a second independent pass the same day.
